measures.t: Increasing the Timeframe for the Hawaii Senate to Consider and Act on Judicial Appointments.
measures.q: Shall the Constitution of the State of Hawaii be amended to allow the Senate more time to consider and act on the appointments of justices and judges, by increasing the timeframe from thirty days to sixty days for appointments made between April 1 and December 31 when the senate is not in regular session or is about to adjourn the regular session?
measures.s:
The proposed amendment would amend article VI, section 3, of the Hawaii State Constitution to extend from thirty days to sixty days the timeframe for Senate consideration of a judicial appointment if the appointment is made between April 1 and December 31, which is typically when the Legislature is nearing adjournment of a regular session or is not in regular session.
The Senate confirmation process for justices and judges of the Hawaii Supreme Court, Intermediate Court of appeals, and Circuit Courts, currently provides that the Governor shall make an appointment within thirty days of receiving a list of nominees from the Judicial Selection Commission. The Senate is then required to consent to or reject the Governor’s appointment within thirty days or be deemed to have consented to the appointment.
Because the Hawaii State Legislature is a part-time legislature and only meets in regular session part of the year, the Senate may need to convene in a special session for the sole purpose of acting on a judicial appointment. The purpose of the amendment is to allow greater flexibility in scheduling special sessions and thus limit the number of special sessions that may be needed to consider judicial appointments.

measures.y: A “yes” vote would extend from thirty days to sixty days the time allowed for the Senate to consider judicial appointments made between April 1 and December 31.
measures.no: A “no” vote would make no change to the Hawaii State Constitution and leave in place the requirement that the Senate consider a judicial appointment within thirty days or be deemed to have consented to the appointment.
measures.r: To pass, the amendment must pass two tests: more YES votes than NO votes, and YES votes from at least half of all the ballots cast in the election, counting ballots left blank or over-voted on this question. measures.t: Directing the Hawaii State Legislature to Establish Procedures for Counties to Issue RISE Bonds, Exempt from County Debt Limits.
measures.q: Shall the Hawaii State Constitution be amended to direct the legislature to authorize the counties to issue resilient infrastructure for shelter and equity bonds to fund public improvements in designated districts, repaid solely by future growth in property tax revenues within those districts, not by increasing real property tax rates, where such bonds are excluded from the counties’ debt limit and are subject to accountability and oversight requirements as may be provided by law?
measures.s:
Article VII, section 12, of the Hawaii State Constitution directs the Hawaii State Legislature to authorize the counties to issue several types of bonds. This amendment to Article VII, section 12, of the Constitution would create a new type of bond called a resilient infrastructure for shelter and equity (RISE) bond and direct the Hawaii State Legislature to establish laws that would allow the counties to issue RISE bonds.
Article VII, section 13, of the Hawaii State Constitution excludes certain types of bonds from the maximum amount of debt that a county is allowed to issue. This amendment to Article VII, section 13, of the Hawaii State Constitution would add RISE bonds to the list of bonds that are excluded when calculating a county’s maximum debt level, making RISE bonds exempt from the counties’ debt limits.
RISE bonds are a form of financing payable solely from incremental increases in real property tax revenue received by a county from designated districts that result from the natural growth of real property values in those districts.
The proposed amendment does not authorize the creation of a new tax nor does it increase property tax rates.

measures.t: Planning Commission Review of General Plan and Land Use Ordinances
measures.q: Shall the Charter be amended, effective January 2, 2027, to provide clarity and consistency in deadlines for planning commission review of revisions to the general plan, zoning ordinances, and other land use ordinances proposed by the council, and transmittal of related findings and recommendations to the council?
measures.s: Currently, the Revised Charter of the County of Maui sets deadlines for a planning commission to transmit its findings and recommendations on proposed land use ordinances and General Plan revisions to the County Council that differ from when the Council can take action on those matters if a planning commission fails to transmit its findings and recommendations. For example, section 8-8.4 of the Charter requires a planning commission to transmit its findings and recommendations on General Plan revisions to the Council within 180 days of the final public hearing on the revisions, and to transmit findings and recommendations on land use ordinances within 120 days of the final public hearing on the ordinance. However, under Section 8-8.6, the Council may approve General Plan revisions and land use ordinances if a planning commission fails to transmit its findings and recommendations within 120 days from when the Council transmits those matters to a planning commission for consideration. This amendment would adjust the time frames for Council action on land use ordinances and General Plan revisions to be consistent with the deadlines for review by a planning commission. This means that the Council could act on revisions to the General Plan if a planning commission fails to transmit its findings and recommendations after 180 days following the final public hearing on the revision. Similarly, the Council could act on land use ordinances if a planning commission fails to transmit its findings and recommendations after 120 days following the final public hearing on the ordinance. Finally, this amendment would require the planning director schedule a public hearing for any Council initiated revisions to the general plan or land use ordinance within 60 days of transmittal to the Planning Department by resolution.

It would also establish a deadline for the Planning Director to schedule public meetings on proposed land use ordinances and revisions to the General Plan.
measures.no: A “no” vote means that current deadlines for planning commission review and time periods for Council action would remain unchanged.

measures.t: Standardizing Deadlines for Voter Initiative, Recall, and Charter Amendment
measures.q: Shall the Charter be amended, effective January 1, 2027, to standardize the deadlines related to the clerk’s processing of petitions related to voter initiative, recall of elected officers or board or commission members, and charter amendments?
measures.s: Under the Revised Charter of Maui, there are three types of petitions to have a measure placed on the ballot for consideration by voters during an election. These include petitions to amend the Maui County Code (also referred to as a “voter initiative”) under Article 11, petitions to recall elected officers or board and commission members under Article 12, and petitions to amend the Charter under Article 14. For all three types of petitions, the County Clerk is responsible for reviewing the sufficiency of the petition, including whether there are a sufficient number of valid voter signatures. Currently, the Charter establishes different deadlines for reviewing the initial petition and supplemental petitions, if any, for all three types of petitions. For voter initiatives, the County Clerk’s Office has 45 days to review the petition, and 20 days to review a supplemental petition. For petitions to recall an elected officer or board or commission member, the County Clerk’s Office has 20 days to review the petition and 10 days to review a supplemental petition. For Charter amendments, the County Clerk’s Office has 15 days to review the petition and there is no provision for supplemental petitions. This amendment would standardize the review period for all three types of petitions to 45 days. The amendment would also increase the review period for supplemental petitions for voter initiatives and recall of an elected officer or board or commission member to 30 days.

measures.no: A “no” vote means that the existing deadlines for reviewing petitions for voter initiatives, recall of elected officers or board or commission members, and charter amendments would remain unchanged.

measures.q: Shall the Charter be amended, effective January 1, 2027, to establish a formula for computing Charter deadlines that excludes weekends and holidays?
measures.s: The Revised Charter of the County of Maui sets various deadlines and time periods in which actions must be taken. On occasion, those deadlines or the end of those time periods fall on days when the County is not open for business, such as Saturdays, Sundays, and holidays. This amendment would adopt a formula for determining deadlines and time periods in the Charter which excludes the first day and includes the last day, unless the last day falls on a Saturday, Sunday, or holiday, in which case the deadline or time period would be extended until 4:30 p.m. on the next business day. This formula would be used to determine all deadlines and time periods in the Charter other than those containing a specific date, or those related to vetoing and overriding vetoes on legislation.

measures.q: Shall the Charter be amended, effective immediately, to repeal the parts of the 2022 Charter amendment that created the Independent Nomination Board and related procedures for nominations for various County officers?
measures.s:
In 2022 the voters of Maui County approved a Charter Amendment establishing the Independent Nomination Board to recruit, evaluate, and nominate candidates for various County boards and commissions, as well as the County Clerk, the County Auditor, the Corporation Counsel, and the Prosecuting Attorney. Nominees for these positions are selected from a list provided by the Independent Nomination Board, unless the Independent Nomination Board fails to meet various deadlines. This amendment would dissolve the Independent Nomination Board and revert to prior methods of nomination and approval for these positions. As a result, the mayor would be able to nominate individuals to fill vacancies on a County board or commission, the Corporation Counsel and the Prosecuting Attorney without having to choose from a list of potential nominees provided by the Independent Nomination Board. The amendment would also allow the Council to appoint the County Clerk and the County Auditor without having to choose from a list of potential nominees provided by the Independent Nomination Board.
In addition, the amendment would: amend deadlines for the mayor to submit nominations for boards and commissions to the Council; amend deadlines for the Council to act on nominations to boards and commissions submitted by the Mayor before they are automatically approved; allow the Council to adopt additional policies on the process for filing vacancies on boards and commissions by ordinance; allows the terms of members on boards and commissions to be set by ordinance; and removes the requirement that notice of public board and commission meetings be published in a newspaper and instead allows for notice to be provided as required by state law.

measures.y: A “yes” vote means that the Independent Nomination Board would be dissolved and the mayor would have authority to nominate members of boards and commissions, as well as the Corporation Counsel, and the Prosecuting Attorney, without having to choose from a list of potential nominees provided by the Independent Nomination Board. The County Clerk and County Auditor would be appointed by the Council without having to choose from a list of potential nominees provided by the Independent Nomination Board. It would also change various deadlines related to the nomination process and allow the Council to adopt additional policies related to boards and commissions by ordinance.
measures.no: A “no” vote means that the Independent Nomination Board and the nomination procedures adopted through the 2022 Charter amendment would remain in effect. Appointments to boards and commissions as well as for the County Clerk, the County Auditor, the Corporation Counsel, and the Prosecuting Attorney would continue to be subject to the existing Independent Nomination Board process.

measures.t: Relating to Zoning Board of Appeals
measures.q: Shall the Kaua‘i County Charter be amended to expedite and clarify the Planning Commission’s appeals process by removing all references to a Zoning Board of Appeals?
measures.s:
PURPOSE
The Zoning Board of Appeals has never been used, and its functions are being handled by Hearings Officers and the Planning Commission. This amendment would remove the Zoning Board of Appeals from the Charter and align the Charter with the current process.
BACKGROUND
The appeals process for the Planning Commission consists of three (3) options. An appeal may be heard by the Planning Commission, a Hearings Officer, or the Zoning Board of Appeals, although the Zoning Board of Appeals has never actually been used.
The Planning Commission has the discretion to conduct the hearing or refer the hearing to a Hearings Officer or the Zoning Board of Appeals. However, the Zoning Board of Appeals has never been put into practice, so appeals are currently managed by the Planning Commission and Hearings Officers. Removing the Zoning Board of Appeals is a recommendation of the Kaua’i County Cost Control Commission to clarify and expedite the appeals process. The Zoning Board of Appeals was added to the charter in 2016, to reduce the workload of the Planning Commission. However, it has proven unworkable to find volunteers willing and able to commit to successive days and sometimes weeks of hearings in highly legalistic procedures. The duration of one hearing consisted of eight (8) hours a day and continued for nine (9) days. As a result, no Zoning Board of Appeals has been installed since it was created. The appeals process is a hearing that is similar to a court proceeding with witnesses, cross-examination, and presentation of evidence. The Hearings Officers are attorneys that are familiar with the legal procedures and rules involved in these hearings. To use a volunteer board of seven people without legal training to conduct these hearings would likely result in more time and more costly court litigation. A neighboring county with a Zoning Board of Appeals is experiencing a two (2) year backlog of hearings and is considering using a Hearings Officer instead.

measures.q: Beginning in 2032, should the City use ranked-choice voting to elect the Mayor, City Council, and Prosecuting Attorney, allowing voters to rank candidates in the order they prefer (1st, 2nd, 3rd, etc.) in a single November election?
measures.s:
PRESENT SITUATION
City officials are elected through a two-step nonpartisan special election. When three or more candidates run for an office, a first special election is conducted with the state primary in August. If a candidate wins a majority, then they are elected. Otherwise, the top two advance to a second special election held with the state general election in November. Turnout in August is typically much lower than in November. This means a relatively small group of voters who may not represent the views of the City as a whole decides the options (or the winners) for everyone else. In the 2024 election, all City officials were elected in August. Additionally, Hawai‘i Revised Statutes section 11-100 limits ranked-choice voting to only special elections to fill City Council vacancies.
IF PROPOSAL PASSES
Beginning in 2032, ranked-choice voting will be used for the Mayor, City Council, and Prosecuting Attorney, and these offices will be decided in the November election by a larger and more representative electorate. Voters can rank any number of candidates in the order they prefer (1st choice, 2nd choice, 3rd choice, etc.). If no candidate receives a majority of first choices, the candidate with the fewest votes is eliminated and those ballots transferred to each voter’s next choice, repeating in rounds until a winner is determined. The City Clerk will also adopt rules and implement a public education program.

measures.q: Should the Charter be amended to require the Honolulu Police Department to 1) adopt policies to ensure the constitutional rights of all persons regardless of immigration or citizenship status are protected, and 2) assist federal immigration enforcement activities only when required by statute or court order, and after the requesting agency’s identity and authority have been confirmed?

It does not establish policies governing the Department’s role in federal immigration enforcement or specify when officers may assist federal immigration authorities. Under Hawaii State Law, Act 141 (2026) prohibits all state and county law enforcement agencies, including the Honolulu Police Department, from providing information to federal immigration authorities for the purposes of immigration enforcement, but does not prohibit the Honolulu Police Department from complying with a judicial warrant, court order, or subpoena.

Law enforcement officers could assist with or facilitate federal immigration enforcement activities only when required by a verifiable state or federal statute or a court order. Before providing assistance, officers would also be required to verify the identity and legal authority of the requesting agency through official channels for each individual action.

measures.q: Should the Charter be amended to clarify that the Affordable Housing Fund is a revolving fund, with repayments, interest, earnings, proceeds, and other receipts derived from the Fund to be redeposited into the Fund?
measures.s:
PRESENT SITUATION
Honolulu voters previously approved an Affordable Housing Fund that provides affordable rental housing for households earning up to sixty percent of the area median income. Housing projects that receive money from the Fund must remain affordable for at least sixty years. The Fund receives roughly eight million dollars per year in property tax revenues, which are used to purchase land, renovate existing buildings, or construct new affordable housing units. Currently the Charter does not specify what happens to money that is loaned from the Affordable Housing Fund and later returns to the City with interest.
Currently, the Charter provides that any funds remaining at the end of any fiscal year shall not lapse. The Charter does not specifically state that repayment, interests, earnings, and proceeds from the Fund are redeposited into the Fund.
IF PROPOSAL PASSES
It would clarify that repayments, interest, earnings and proceeds derived from the Fund are redeposited into the Fund. The Affordable Housing Fund could support a wider range of affordable rental housing, including affordable units within developments that contain a variety of uses (mixed-use) and price points for housing (mixed-income). Loan repayments, interest earnings, and other revenues generated by the Fund would remain available for future affordable housing investments, so that the Fund can grow and support more affordable housing units and projects over time.

measures.q: Should the Charter be amended to no longer require a second public hearing for any transaction related to City real property interests?
measures.s:
PRESENT SITUATION
The Charter requires the Department of Housing and Land Management to hold a public hearing to determine whether each real property transaction or activity related to city real property interests serves the public interest. Additionally, they impose significant costs on the City in staff time and advertising expenses. For transactions or activities affecting a City real property interest that exceeds one-quarter acre in size, the Department is also required to conduct a public hearing in the Council district where the real property interest is located. The Charter also requires the Department to prepare a report for each transaction or activity with specific findings that it serves the public interest, which must be approved by the Council.
IF PROPOSAL PASSES
A separate public hearing requirement for City real property transactions will no longer be required, but the public will retain the ability to learn about and testify on all City property transactions when they appear on the agenda for City Council meetings.

measures.q: Should quorum and board action be based on the majority of members eligible to vote, excluding vacancies and non-voting members?
measures.s:
PRESENT SITUATION
A majority of all members to which the board or commission is entitled constitutes a quorum, unless specified in the law or ordinance creating the board or commission or in any other law or ordinance. The Charter also currently requires a majority of the entire membership to take any action, and the entire membership has been interpreted to include vacancies and members who are not eligible to vote. As a result, some boards and commissions with vacancies and nonvoting members have been unable to take official action despite having enough members present to conduct a meeting.
IF PROPOSAL PASSES
The amendment would clarify that vacancies and non-voting members are excluded when determining whether a quorum is present and that, once a quorum has been established, official actions may be approved by a majority of the members present and voting, unless state law or the Charter itself requires a higher voting threshold. Neighborhood Boards, which are elected positions, would not be affected by this change.

measures.q: Should the First Deputy of the Department of Human Resources be exempt from civil service provisions, like similar roles in other City departments?
measures.s:
PRESENT SITUATION
The First Deputy of the Department of Human Resources is a civil service employee. They also represent the City in negotiations with unions over civil service salaries, benefits, and privileges. In all other counties in the State, the same position is exempt from the civil service, as are first deputies in other city departments in the City and County of Honolulu.
IF PROPOSAL PASSES
The position of First Deputy of the Department of Human Resources will become an appointed position exempt from the civil service. This will make the position consistent with other counties and City departments effective January 1, 2027.

measures.q: Should the City Clerk be required to provide technical and secretarial services to the Charter Commission?
measures.s:
PRESENT SITUATION
The Charter requires the appointment of a Charter Commission every ten years to review City government and recommend Charter amendments. The Charter does not designate a permanent administrative home or guarantee technical or secretarial support for the Commission.
IF PROPOSAL PASSES
The City Clerk would be required to provide administrative and technical support to the Charter Commission. The Charter Commission’s authority, responsibilities, independence, and ability to propose Charter amendments for voter consideration would not change.

measures.q: Should the Charter make a Councilmember, the Mayor, or the Prosecuting Attorney ineligible for election to any City office for two years if impeached, or if the official resigns after an impeachment petition has been filed, consistent with the provision for being recalled from office?
measures.s:
PRESENT SITUATION
Currently, a Councilmember, the Mayor, and the Prosecuting Attorney may still be elected or appointed to any other City office with no restrictions even if they have been removed from office pursuant to impeachment proceedings, or if they resign after an impeachment petition has been filed.
IF PROPOSAL PASSES
A Councilmember, Mayor, or Prosecuting Attorney who is impeached, or who resigns after an impeachment petition is filed, could not be elected or appointed to any City office for two years. This would make the restriction similar to the one that already applies to elected officials removed through a recall election.

methods: lists

Who is running comes only from the State of Hawaii Office of Elections’ own lists of candidates for the November 3 general election and the August 8 primary, and the official primary results; each file is named below, with where it was read. The U.S. Senate and House races are on the Congress pages. County and local contests are read from the lists named below too: which local offices are on this ballot, what was read and what is not here yet are set out under County by county, in the words of the notes kept with the lists.
lists

What is read. From those lists this site reads only the office, the district, the county and the city, town or district a contest belongs to, the candidate’s name, the party, the ballot order where the list gives one, and the primary vote counts. Addresses, phone numbers, e-mail and websites, where a list carries them, are never read, kept or shown. No photos, ages, biographies or campaign money are shown for state and local candidates.
lists

Parties. Offices elected on party lines show the party each candidate filed under, written out. The Office of Hawaiian Affairs Trustee, At-Large, the Office of Hawaiian Affairs Trustee, Maui Resident and the Office of Hawaiian Affairs Trustee, Oahu Resident are on the nonpartisan ballot; the page says so instead of a party. Every county and local contest here is for a nonpartisan office; the page says so instead of a party.
lists

Primaries. Where more people ran in a primary (August 8) than it could send on, everyone on that primary ballot is shown, with who went on to November, read from the general election list. Vote counts are the official results where they are loaded; where they are not, the race says so.
lists
Order. The lists read here give no ballot order. Candidates appear by surname. Never by money, polls or party.
holders

Who holds a seat today (the Legislature and the statewide offices the roster carries) comes from the Open States roster the record side of this site uses. A candidate matched to a sitting legislator by district and name, one fit only, links to their record page and nothing more.
maps

Maps and “use my location”. District lines are the Census Bureau’s cartographic boundary files (2024 Census Bureau cartographic boundary files), the lines the state pages draw, and the county lines are the Bureau’s too (2024 Census Bureau cartographic boundary file (counties, 1:500,000)); your county’s sample ballot is the authority on your district. Your location is worked out on your own device and never sent anywhere; a rounded copy (about half a mile) is kept on the device, with your choices, until you tap “Forget”. A typed address goes from your device straight to the U.S. Census Bureau’s address finder, only when you press Look up; only the spot it finds comes back, used the same way, and this site never sees or keeps the address.
page
Nobody is scored or graded. The cards show the record; the judging is yours.
polls

Polls of the statewide races are shown only from pollsters in the American Association for Public Opinion Research’s Transparency Initiative, who publish how each poll was done: the latest from up to five of them, each checked against the pollster’s own release, and our own average of the ten most recent, with the arithmetic shown. Polls by other pollsters are counted and named, not shown. A poll is a measure of opinion when it was taken, with a margin of error, not a forecast.
polls

Betting markets. Prices on Polymarket, a prediction market, are shown for the statewide races it lists, as information only: not a poll, not a forecast and not an official record. They are read from its public data, and prices move all day. Where Kalshi or PredictIt (two other markets) lists a race, the page says so and links to it, but shows none of its prices: their terms do not allow other sites to show them. A notice comes before any link to a market. The Civic Archive takes no money from any market and uses no referral links.
lists

The contests for Congress at the top of your ballot are the Congress pages’ own, from the state’s official candidate list: each name as printed, with its party label, in the ballot order the list gives (or by surname where it gives none), with its write-in and incumbent marks. Everything else about those candidates is on their race’s Congress page. Your U.S. House district is found from the Census Bureau’s 119th Congress lines, the ones the Congress pages draw, on your own device.
rules

Ballot questions. Each question’s official texts are shown word for word: the question as it will be printed and, where the record has them, the official summary, what a yes and a no vote do and the fiscal note, each labelled by who wrote it where the record says, and by its source. Where this site puts something in its own words (often the votes needed to pass and how the question got on the ballot), the question’s page says so beside it. Each side’s arguments in the official voter guide are linked, never reprinted.
page

Your ballot, printed or kept. “As it will look” draws your ballot as a printed sample ballot; it is a preview, not an official ballot, and your county’s own sample ballot is the authority. “Keep this ballot on my phone” saves the contests, the names, the questions’ words and the names of your districts and places in this device’s own storage, with the date, to open with no signal. No location, no address and no account: nothing is sent anywhere. “Forget my location and choices” removes it, and so does “Forget this ballot” on the kept page. Anyone holding your unlocked phone can see which districts a kept ballot is for.

items: Wisconsin's past results are here: Congress, the Legislature, district attorneys, statewide questions, and Milwaukee and Dane counties' own offices and questions, from the state Elections Commission's official files.

Minnesota now has every local contest of 2020, 2022 and 2024: judges, county offices, cities, townships, school boards, soil and water and hospital districts, and local questions, read from the Secretary of State's own result files (as kept by the Internet Archive after the count was certified) and checked precinct by precinct against the certified results.

changelog.title: Past results for every state, and the ballot in Spanish (a draft)
items: Past results now cover 49 states and the District of Columbia: the November general elections of 2020, 2022 and 2024, from President down to county offices, cities, townships, school boards, special districts and ballot questions wherever the state or county publishes official figures. Wisconsin's official files are not reachable yet, and the page says so.

Figures are shown by county and by city or town. Where a state's figures come from a compilation rather than its own official count, they are labelled secondary and no winner is marked from them. Where two official records disagree, both are shown and nothing is changed.
Each race page's "This seat before" now finds past elections in every loaded state.

On the draft site only: the ballot pages, menus, Help and the reading settings can be read in Spanish ("¿Leer en español?"). Each translated page says it was translated by Claude, an AI model, and not yet reviewed by a person. Names, office titles as printed and the words on your ballot stay in English; office titles show a Spanish translation beside the official English.
Ballot pages now say in one plain sentence what each office does, at the Beginner and Easy levels, with the official sources one tap away.

changelog.title: Past results: how places and seats voted in 2020, 2022 and 2024
items: New in Election Night: "Past results". Pick a state and a year (the November general elections of 2024, 2022 and 2020), then any contest on that ballot: names and parties as printed, votes and shares, the certified total and where it comes from, a county map, and the figures for each county, city or township.

North Dakota and Iowa are here in full, down to county offices, townships, soil and water districts and every ballot question. Illinois has Congress, the Legislature, judges and the statewide questions; Minnesota has President, Congress, the Legislature, Governor and the statewide offices. Their county and local races are next, and the page says which parts are still missing.

On The Ballot: race pages now have "This seat before", the same seat's past elections, with a note when the district's lines were different then. Ballot question pages have "Questions voters here decided before".
Every figure comes from the state's or county's official certified count and was checked against the official totals. Where two official records disagree, both are shown and nothing is changed.

changelog.title: The dashboard
items: New: a dashboard of the whole record, in three views. "Your place at a glance" shows any state or the whole country: what is on its ballot, who holds its seats, its ballot questions, and a link to its mail-voting facts. "The record, filtered" turns Congress's bills and floor votes into a sentence and charts you can narrow by chamber, topic and year. "Every state, side by side" puts all the states on one map, one measure at a time, with a two-state comparison.

Every figure is counted from the site's records when the page is built, and every chart says where its numbers come from and what they cannot tell you. Places can be compared; people are never ranked.
Beginner shows a few plain tiles; Medium adds the charts; Advanced opens the sources. Each view has its own address and a Share button.
The dashboard is linked from the home page, the menus, the On The Ballot door and Help.

changelog.title: Vote by mail, and questions answered
items: Every state's ballot page now has "Vote by mail or absentee": the last day to ask for a mail ballot and the last day to send it back for November 3, how to ask (the state's own link), how to send it back, what the envelope needs, how to track it, early voting in person, and what the state says for students at school elsewhere in the state or in another state, and for military and overseas voters. Every fact links to the state's own page or law and shows when it was checked. When a deadline has passed, the page says so and points to voting early or on Election Day.
"Your ballot" now says, under the election date, when to ask for a mail ballot.
The Congress ballot pages link each state to its mail-voting facts.

New: On The Ballot's questions page, with plain answers on voting by mail, students, military and overseas voters, moving, checking your registration, finding your polling place, when polls close, early voting, ID, tracking your ballot and a spoiled or lost ballot. Pick your state and each answer uses its own rules.
Every fact comes from the state's own election office or law, or from federal voting sites, and a second check re-read each source. The state election office always has the final word.

changelog.title: Share anything
items: Every part of the site now has a Share button: pages, races, ballot questions, counties, members, bills, votes, maps, the district lenses and Election Night. On a phone it opens your phone's own share sheet. On a computer it offers Copy link, e-mail, Facebook, LinkedIn, X, Bluesky, WhatsApp and Reddit (and text messages on a phone).
Nothing is sent until you pick a place. The place you pick then sees the link. No sharing buttons from those companies are loaded on these pages.
Every race, ballot question and county, down to the local contests, now has its own preview picture, so a shared link shows what it is about.
"Share my ballot" shares your precinct's ballot, after a note saying the link shows roughly where you vote. A shared link never carries your exact location.
The ready-made message sticks to the facts, for example: "U.S. Senate, Minnesota: who is on the November 3 ballot, from the official list."
